title: Making a leather axe mask and knife sheath
subtitle: Shape and stitch a fitted leather protector for an axe blade head and a belt-carry sheath for a fixed-blade knife from vegetable-tanned leather
excerpt: How to make a leather axe mask and a belt knife sheath from 3-4 mm vegetable-tanned leather. Covers tracing tool outlines, cutting the leather, adding a welt, punching stitching holes, saddle-stitching, fitting a snap fastener, and conditioning.
sourceNotes: Traditional leathercraft and bushcraft tool-carry practice, public domain. Standard saddlery and harness-making references (public domain).

glossaryTerms.definition: A strip of leather sandwiched between the two face panels of a sheath or holster at the edges, creating a gap that gives the blade clearance inside the sheath without pressing on the stitch line. The welt also reinforces the edge stitching so the blade cannot cut through to the threads.

A hand stitching method using two needles threaded onto opposite ends of a single waxed thread. Both needles pass through the same hole from opposite sides, creating a diagonal interlocking stitch that is stronger and more durable than machine lock-stitch, and will not unravel if a stitch breaks.

content.text: A leather axe mask covers the axe blade head for safe storage and carries the axe securely. A belt sheath for a fixed-blade knife protects both blade and user. Both are made from 3 to 4 mm vegetable-tanned leather, using a
. INTERMEDIATE: accurate stitch spacing and consistent thread tension are the key skills.
Trace the tool and make the pattern

Lay the axe head or knife blade on card and trace the outline. Add 10 mm clearance around the blade outline for the sheath body. For the axe mask, trace only the head section from the shoulder to the bit (cutting edge). For the knife sheath, include the handle block if the sheath covers the handle to the guard.
Cut the leather panels and welt

Cut two matching face panels from 3 to 4 mm leather using the card template and the leatherwork knife guided along the card edge. Cut the welt strip: a 12 to 15 mm wide strip the same length as the edge to be stitched. Bevel all edges with the edge beveller to reduce stiffness at the outer edge. Dampen the leather slightly for easier shaping if the panels need to curve around the tool.

Sandwich the welt between the two face panels along the edge to be stitched, with all three layers aligned. Use a stitching groover to mark the stitch line 4 to 5 mm from the edge. Punch the stitch holes through all three layers at once using a pricking iron and mallet, spacing holes at 4 mm intervals. Punch on an end-grain wooden block to get clean holes.

Thread a length of waxed thread with a needle on each end. Pass the first needle through the first hole, leaving equal thread on both sides. Pass the second needle through the same hole in the opposite direction, crossing the threads. Continue along the stitch line, keeping equal tension on both threads so the diagonal stitch pattern is even. Finish by stitching back through the last two holes and trimming the thread ends.

Apply a thin coat of neatsfoot oil or beeswax leather conditioner to all surfaces. For the axe mask, fit a two-part snap fastener through a tab that folds over the mask opening to keep it secure during carry. Set the snap with a snap setter and anvil.

attrs.symptom: Stitch tension is uneven: some stitches lie flat and others twist
attrs.cause: Unequal pull on the two needles, or one needle crossed over the other incorrectly.
attrs.fix: Pull both needles to equal tension after each stitch. Check that the crossing pattern (first needle always passes in front of the second, or always behind) is consistent throughout.

attrs.symptom: Leather panels are too stiff to press together at a curved section
attrs.cause: The leather is too thick for the curve radius, or was not dampened before shaping.
attrs.fix: Dampen the area with warm water and press the curve into shape over a round form. Allow to dry in position before stitching.
